forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Croydon draft budget cuts exceptional support need by £63m, leaving £287.5m-£331.5m to 2030-31
news_drafts.lead:
Croydon Council's draft budget for 2027-28 would reduce the exceptional financial support it needs by £63m from the estimate made in July. This is government permission to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending, and is a last resort. Even so, the papers before Cabinet on 14 October put the total requirement over the four years to 2030-31 at between £287.5m and £331.5m.

The reduction follows £83.7m of savings the council has identified, with a further £6m to £17m possible. The council's medium-term financial strategy, its plan for the next four years, describes the requirement as "in the region of £300m over the period to 2030/31, with an ongoing annual requirement of at least £60m thereafter". The annual figure settles at between £59.3m and £70.3m from 2030-31. The council states that it is difficult to see a route out without government intervention.

The strategy's service-by-service appendix sets out the year-by-year profile: £119m in 2026-27 and £120.7m in 2027-28, falling to £82.8m in 2028-29, £75.7m in 2029-30 and £76.3m in 2030-31.

news_drafts.headline: Croydon's forecast 2026-27 overspend falls £0.8m to £2.3m at period 3
news_drafts.lead:
Croydon Council is forecasting a £2.3m overspend on its General Fund (the day-to-day budget for most services) for 2026-27, down from £3.1m a period earlier. The period 3 report to the Executive Mayor and Cabinet on 23 September says this shows action to control spending "is already having an impact". The £485.4m budget still relied on £119m of capitalisation directions, which is government permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending so it can be paid for by borrowing. The report puts the future cost at about £85,000 a year for every £1m.

Interest payable is forecast at £50.7m against a £55.9m budget. The council has delivered a forecast £26.5m of its £34.7m savings target, 76.4%, leaving £8.2m not on track. Children's social care is forecast to overspend by £3.4m. Placements account for £1.7m of that on a £49.7m budget, and the dearest single placement in June cost £14,004 a week. Holding vacancies produced a £0.9m staffing underspend. In the housing revenue account (the ring-fenced account for council homes, paid for by rents), a £3.9m overspend is attributed to repairs and safety works, which are £2.8m over, and to disrepair claims.

The report forecasts a £45m overspend on high needs, the school funding for children with special educational needs, in 2026-27. The deficit on the dedicated schools grant stood at £67.5m on 31 March 2026. The council says it could reach £96m when the statutory override, the government rule keeping such deficits off councils' main balance sheets, ends in March 2028.

A separate paper sets out four options for cutting working-age Council Tax Support, which would save between £3.6m and £11.9m a year, including the Greater London Authority's share. The scheme costs about £39m a year, with the council bearing about £20m. The paper says collection could fall from 98.0% to 97.5%.

news_drafts.headline: Croydon's debt servicing costs force reliance on Government support to balance budget
news_drafts.lead: Croydon spent £82m servicing its £1.5bn General Fund debt in 2025/26, according to its annual governance statement. The council required £108.7m of capitalisation directions from Government — permission to treat day-to-day spending as capital spending and pay for it through borrowing — to balance its budget. The external auditor has rated the council's financial sustainability Red, the lowest possible rating, citing significant weakness in the council's arrangements for debt and cost reduction. An auditor's statutory recommendation, carried forward from the prior year unchanged, states the council must work with newly appointed Commissioners to develop measures enabling reduced operating costs and return to self-sufficiency, and that "a solution to the debt issue is vital" to assess the council's capability to manage its finances sustainably.

findings.headline: Council undertaking task and finish exercise on unaccompanied children cost pressures with other national entry port councils (Hillingdon, Kent)
findings.detail: The council recognises it faces disproportionate cost pressures from high numbers of care experienced former unaccompanied children. It is undertaking a joint task and finish group exercise with Hillingdon and Kent County Council to review cost pressures and consider the impact on care experienced grant allocation from central government and local authority housing need.
findings.matters: Indicates structural cost pressure from asylum/immigration-related placement demand; councils are jointly investigating whether this affects grant distribution formulas
findings.figures: No figures given; this is a policy review exercise
findings.quote: Review policy and practice and undertake a task and finish group exercise to review our own cost pressures and the cost pressures of Hillingdon and Kent County Council (as national entry ports) to consider the disproportionate impact that having high numbers of Care Experienced former unaccompanied children has on the care experienced grant allocation from central government and the need for local authority housing.

findings.headline: New temporary accommodation strategy caps use of private landlords above set rates; incorporated in £11.7m housing savings target
findings.detail: A new temporary accommodation strategy was presented to Cabinet in September 2026. It includes limiting use of landlords above new capped rates, forming part of the council's £11.7m housing savings target for demand and cost management.
findings.matters: Significant savings (£11.7m) contingent on managing temporary accommodation costs through supply and rate controls; a material revenue lever
findings.quote: Limit the use of landlords above the new TA capped levels

findings.headline: London Living Wage contractual requirement removed from future external contracts; providers to apply market-based indexing instead
findings.detail: The council is ending its London Living Wage commitment in external contracts going forward. Future contracts will apply indexing relating to market conditions rather than the London Living Wage floor, representing a strategic shift in approach to care provider workforce costs across the supply chain.
findings.matters: Represents a strategic shift in council approach to contracted care provider costs; affects future contracting for adult social care in London
findings.quote: Remove LLW contractual clause from future provider contracts. Services to offer the appropriate indexing relating to market conditions.

findings.headline: Council rejected staff pay freeze, citing risks to recruitment, retention and likelihood of increased agency staff costs eroding savings
findings.detail: The council consciously rejected proposals for a general pay freeze or requirement for chief officers to forego national pay awards. The stated rationale was that such measures would damage staff morale, make recruitment and retention more difficult, and likely lead to increased agency staff usage that would quickly erase any savings achieved.
findings.matters: Indicates council's assessment of pay/staffing cost trade-offs and explicit concern about agency cost escalation if pay is constrained
findings.figures: No quantification; this is a policy rejection rather than a budgeted decision
findings.quote: It would also make future recruitment and retention of high-calibre staff more challenging. This would in turn likely lead to increased usage of agency staff to fill essential roles, eroding savings achieved, potentially quite quickly and substantially.

findings.headline: Council Tax Support Scheme consultation launched September 2026; potential saving of £2.9m to £9.5m depends entirely on consultation outcomes
findings.detail: A Cabinet report launching statutory consultation on Council Tax Support Scheme changes went to Cabinet in September 2026. The level of potential saving depends on the consultation process and options chosen. Changes can only be made for working-age claimants; the pensioners scheme is set nationally.
findings.matters: Significant financial dependency on consultation outcomes with a threefold range; timing and scope are constrained by statutory requirements
findings.quote: Cabinet report to launch statutory consultation went to September 2026 Cabinet meeting. Level of potential saving will depend on consultation and resulting options for change. Can only change for working age claimants, pensioners scheme is set nationally.
